beats.script_body: The man most responsible for founding these squares in the 1830s was a lawyer and visionary real estate investor named Samuel Ruggles. Correctly anticipating New York's growth uptown, Ruggles bought up undeveloped plots in the area that would become Union Square and Gramercy Park, hoping to entice the wealthy to settle around exclusive, fenced parks at each square's center. The value of his property climbed after the Great Fire of 1835 pushed Manhattanites uptown in large numbers. Union Square opened in 1839 with an oval-shaped iron fence around its central park. Ruggles built himself a four-story home here — though his true masterpiece, where he never actually lived, was Gramercy Park.

beats.source_passage: The man most responsible for the founding of these squares in the 1830s was the lawyer and visionary real estate investor, Samuel Ruggles. At that time, the area between Fourteenth and Twenty-eighth Streets had begun to take shape as a genteel suburb on the northern outskirts of the city. Correctly anticipating New York's impending growth uptown, Ruggles purchased numerous undeveloped plots of land in the area that would become Union Square and Gramercy Park. Ruggles saw an opportunity to beautify these suburban communities and turn them into neighborhoods for the city's elite. By designing an exclusive, fenced park in the center of each square, Ruggles hoped to entice the wealthy to settle around them. The value of Ruggles's property grew after the Great Fire of 1835 prompted Manhattanites to migrate uptown in large numbers. In 1839, Union Square opened with an oval-shaped iron fence surrounding the park at its center. Ruggles built a four-story home for himself at Union Square, but his masterpiece, although he never lived there himself, was Gramercy Park, which opened in 1844.

beats.script_body: Although Union Square was New York's most fashionable shopping and theater district in the late nineteenth century, it fell into a long decline beginning in the 1920s. The department stores and boutiques of 'Ladies' Mile' moved further uptown, and the square, caught between the midtown and downtown business districts, was left to deteriorate. By the 1960s and 1970s it was known as a haunt for drug dealers and the homeless. A $3.6 million reconstruction project launched in 1985 dramatically refurbished the park's neglected landscape and addressed its safety problems. Crowning that restoration, Union Square Park was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1997.

beats.source_passage: Although it was New York's most fashionable shopping and theater district in the late nineteenth century, Union Square experienced a long period of decline beginning in the 1920s. The department stores and boutiques that made up "Ladies Mile" moved further uptown, closer to the upscale residential districts of the Upper East and West Sides. Caught between the midtown and downtown business districts, Union Square and its environs were left to deteriorate. Union Square became known in the 1960s and 1970s as a site for drug dealers and a place for the homeless. A $3.6 million reconstruction project, launched in 1985, dramatically refurbished the park's neglected landscape and successfully addressed its safety problems. Crowning its restoration, Union Square Park was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1997 by the National Parks Service.

beats.script_body: The nickname 'Ladies' Mile' took on a far different meaning after dark. Above the department stores along Broadway lay lavishly furnished brothels catering to upper-class men. These high-priced 'Temples of Love' advertised themselves in publications such as the Gentleman's Directory, promising women who were beautiful, charming, and refined conversationalists. Outside the elite brothels, throngs of streetwalkers worked Ladies' Mile after dark. By the 1890s, reformers complained that both Union and Stuyvesant Square Parks had become a place where, in their words, 'tramps both male and female haggle and dispute over their price.'

beats.script_body: The proliferation of department stores along Broadway from Ninth to Twenty-third Street earned this stretch the nickname 'Ladies' Mile' in the 1870s. It began when A. T. Stewart built a massive cast-iron emporium filling an entire block at Broadway and East Ninth Street, selling expensive furnishings, antiques, fabrics, and women's wear. His triumph drew a succession of upscale stores: Tiffany and Company demolished James Renwick Jr.'s Church of the Puritans at Union Square to build its store in 1869, while Lord & Taylor's, Arnold Constable's, and W. & J. Sloane's filled out the avenue. Macy's and B. Altman's opened two blocks west on Sixth Avenue.

The shopping district also included a stretch of Sixth Avenue two blocks west, where Macy's and B. Altman's opened.

beats.script_body: While Broadway brought department stores, Union Square's other tributary — the Bowery — brought theaters. New York Sun reporter Ted McAlpin dubbed the district 'the Rialto,' and by the 1870s Union Square had replaced the Bowery as the hub of theater activity in the city. In 1854 the Academy of Music, one of the largest theaters in the world, opened on Fourteenth Street near the square. As the city's primary opera house it hosted the American premieres of Aida, Lohengrin, Die Walküre, and Carmen. All of New York society pined for the prestige of an opera box; despite a cost of as much as $30,000, the waiting list was long and included names like Vanderbilt, Astor, and Gould.

beats.script_body: Some called Union Square Park the 'slave market,' because aspiring actors bargained for contracts with theater managers in impromptu negotiations right in the park. The Rialto's restaurants became legends in their own right — Luchow's, opened in 1882, was a hot spot where celebrities and performers mingled and danced while critics wrote their reviews at the dinner tables. The popular tune 'Yes Sir, That's My Baby' is said to have been written one drunken night by Gus Kahn on a Luchow's tablecloth.

beats.script_body: At the south side of the park stands Henry Kirke Brown's George Washington, dedicated on July 4, 1856, and considered by some the finest equestrian statue in the country. It depicts Washington's triumphant return to New York City on November 25, 1783, as British troops ended their seven-year occupation at the close of the Revolutionary War. Washington came personally to repossess the city he had lost to the British in 1776, and at this very spot he and his officers were greeted by a crowd of jubilant citizens. The site was then known as Union Place, a grassy clearing north of the city named for the juncture of the Boston Post Road — later the Bowery — and the Albany Post Road, later Broadway. As the statue depicts, Washington then headed southward down the path of the Albany Post Road toward the city, accompanied by the cheering crowd, while New Yorkers thronged the streets to catch a glimpse of him. For years afterward, the anniversary of that day was celebrated in New York as 'Evacuation Day.'

beats.script_body: K. B. Patel's statue of Mohandas K. Gandhi, from 1986, stands in a floral bed known as the Gandhi Garden to the southwest of the park, where Fourteenth Street and Broadway meet. Donated by the citizens of India, it was originally meant for Washington Market Park in TriBeCa, but residents there rejected it. It is fitting that the great practitioner of nonviolent protest is honored at Union Square instead, which has a long tradition of mostly peaceful protest.

beats.script_body: On September 5, 1882, the nation's first Labor Day parade ended at Union Square after marching up Broadway from City Hall. From then on, the square became the preferred site of labor rallies and mass political protests. Soapbox orators regularly drew crowds, and thousands turned out for every May Day and Labor Day. The anarchist Isadore Wisotsky later recalled the atmosphere of the 1910s: 'We gathered to make revolution and stayed to talk. And how we talked — anarchism, atheism, against the military, for birth control, against injustice, for socialism and for the rights of workers to organize. The right to speak at Union Square was more precious than the bread we sweated to earn.'

beats.script_body: One of the most tension-filled protests at Union Square came on the night of August 22, 1927, when five thousand people gathered for a candlelight vigil for the anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti, about to be executed in Boston. The police were so afraid of violence that they stationed machine guns on the roof of Klein's department store nearby — but no incidents occurred. A few years later, though, police and protestors battled in a bloody riot here on March 6, 1930. Demonstrators had come, six months after the 1929 stock market crash, to mark International Unemployment Day, an event sponsored by the American Communist Party. When thousands tried to march down Broadway without a permit, the police met them with force, igniting a violent conflict that left hundreds injured.

beats.script_body: Directly in front of the band shell stands Henry Kirke Brown's Abraham Lincoln, dedicated at Union Square in 1868 and believed to be the first public statue of Lincoln erected in the country. Unlike Brown's masterful Washington at the opposite end of the park, this statue was not well received. With his rumpled clothes and plain demeanor, Brown's Lincoln may have accurately captured the historical man, but it was deemed uninspiring — the outpouring of emotion after Lincoln's assassination on Good Friday 1865 had raised the fallen president to an almost Christlike stature in the popular mind. In Brown's rendering, the solemn Lincoln holds a rolled speech — or perhaps the Emancipation Proclamation — in his left hand, hanging calmly and unheroically at his side.

beats.script_body: Union Square is a fitting place to honor Lincoln, for it was during the Civil War that the square became the central gathering place in the city — the Times Square of the nineteenth century. After the fall of Fort Sumter, Lincoln's call for volunteers was answered by thousands of young men who flocked to enlist at recruiting tents that dotted the interior of the park. Nearly a quarter-million people gathered here on Saturday, April 20, 1861, to hear speakers denounce the Southern rebellion, while the tattered American flag rescued from Fort Sumter waved from the George Washington statue, where it had been patriotically placed.

beats.script_body: On the south side of Fourteenth Street, an apartment complex completed in 1998 carries on its facade an elaborate $3 million artwork titled Metronome. Unveiled in September 1999, it is a jumble of symbols its creators, Andrew Ginzel and Kristin Jones, called 'an ode to the impossibility of knowing time.' It features fifteen digital numbers counting the time elapsing from midnight, a black-and-gold sphere that rotates with the phases of the moon, and a five-foot opening that periodically belches blasts of steam. In a whimsical nod to the neighborhood, the artists cast the disembodied hand reaching out from the top of Metronome from Henry Kirke Brown's statue of George Washington across the street.

Unveiled in September 1999, Metronome is a jumble of symbols that has been described by its creators, Andrew Gizel and Kristen Jones, as "an ode to the impossibility of knowing time." It features fifteen digital numbers that count off the time elapsing from midnight, a black and gold sphere that rotates in synchronization with the phases of the moon, and a five-foot opening that periodically belches blasts of steam. In a whimsical nod to its neighborhood surroundings, Gizel and Hones cast the disembodied hand that stretches forth from the top Metronome from Henry Kirke Brown's statue of George Washington across the street.

beats.script_body: On the east side of the square stands the statue of the French general Marquis de Lafayette, done in 1873 by Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi — the same man who designed the Statue of Liberty. Lafayette served as a major general on George Washington's staff, and an inscription on the pedestal quotes his words: 'As soon as I heard of American Independence my heart was enlisted.' In 1824, at the invitation of Congress, Lafayette returned to America and was warmly embraced as the toast of New York society. He was the first foreigner ever granted honorary American citizenship — the second being Winston Churchill.

beats.script_body: At the corner of Seventeenth Street and Park Avenue, the New York Film Academy is housed in the last of the Tammany Hall headquarters, built in 1929 during the administration of Mayor Jimmy Walker. Walker, the last mayor elevated to power by Tammany Hall, embodied the flashy style of the affluent 1920s. The construction of this federal-style building was financed by Wall Street investments — but the stock market crash that ruined those investors later that year also helped bring about the downfall of Tammany Hall itself. In 1933, New Yorkers elected a Republican mayor, Fiorello La Guardia, who promised to destroy Tammany forever.

beats.script_body: The Society of St. Tammany, or Columbian Order, was formed in 1788, taking its name from the legendary Delaware Indian chief Tamanend, adopted as the club's patron saint. The organization loved pseudo–American Indian titles: 'sachems' for council members, 'braves' for the rank and file, 'wigwam' for headquarters. Under Aaron Burr it became a Jeffersonian club, and later, under Martin Van Buren, a Jacksonian Democratic one. Its real power came from a grassroots alliance with immigrant voters, built on graft: local 'bosses' dispensed financial aid and protection in exchange for votes. In the 1860s, Tammany's 'Grand Sachem' William M. 'Boss' Tweed used the machine autocratically to control patronage while embezzling millions; the exposure of the Tweed ring in 1871 scandalized the nation. Yet Tammany endured as a defender of the working man and a patronage engine well into the 1930s, facilitating the careers of Governor Alfred E. Smith and Mayor Jimmy Walker — both sons of Irish immigrants. Perhaps its ethic was best summed up by sachem George Washington Plunkitt, who explained his vast wealth by saying: 'I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.'

beats.script_body: At 109–111 East Fifteenth Street stands the oldest surviving clubhouse in the city — the Century Association Building, now the Century Center for Performing Arts, designed by Charles Gambrill and Henry Hobson Richardson in 1869. The Century Association, formed in 1847, brought together men 'of all guilds' to cultivate 'a taste for Letters and the Arts and social enjoyment,' aspiring to become the American equivalent of the French Academy — though in reality it remained more about socializing than serious discussion. In the 1880s, William Watson Gilder, the first editor of Century magazine, borrowed his journal's name without permission from the Century Club, of which he was a member.

The building's most majestic feature is the Tower of Light, a massive clock tower added in 1926, most impressive when brilliantly illuminated at night.

beats.script_body: Arriving at Stuyvesant Square from Fifteenth Street, the first landmarks to grab your attention are the red-brick Friends Meeting House and Seminary to your left, dating from 1860. Part of a five-building complex that also includes the original schoolhouse, an elegant nineteenth-century townhouse across Fifteenth Street, and a modern school building, the Friends Seminary dominates the southwest corner of the square. A doctrinal split in the Quaker community prompted the construction of this meetinghouse, when one group seceded from another congregation a few blocks away at Gramercy Park. When the two groups reconciled in 1958, the Gramercy Park congregation abandoned their building to join this one.

beats.script_body: Across Sixteenth Street from the Friends Meeting House stands St. George's Episcopal Church, completed in 1856 — one of the earliest examples of Romanesque revival architecture in America. The brownstone exterior, by Otto Blesch, had to be restored after the church was badly damaged in an 1865 fire; Leopold Eidlitz, who designed the original interior, rebuilt it according to Blesch's original plans. The two spires were never properly restored and were finally torn down in 1888. Next door, on the north side, is St. George's Chapel of 1911, a fine Gothic revival companion to the older building.

beats.script_body: The four-acre twin parks of Stuyvesant Square are bisected by Second Avenue, whose traffic makes a noisy invasion of an otherwise pastoral setting. The extension of Second Avenue through the park was part of the original plan when Peter Gerard Stuyvesant deeded the land to the city in 1836 — for just five dollars — though no one could have foreseen the volume of traffic that would later speed down the avenue. The cast-iron fence that surrounds each section of the park dates from 1850. Stuyvesant Square, and all the land from Twentieth to Fifth Street, lay within the farm of Peter Stuyvesant back in the 1650s.

Dvořák lived on East Seventeenth Street, within sight of this spot, while serving as director of the National Conservatory of Music from 1892 to 1895. During that time he composed the acclaimed symphony From the New World — his tribute to the music of America.

beats.script_body: By the 1890s, Stuyvesant Square had become a small, wealthy enclave of American-born residents amid a growing immigrant population of Jews and Catholics moving up from the Lower East Side. St. George's Parish was dominated for decades by its senior warden, the banker J. P. Morgan — one of the most powerful men in the world. When the neighborhood's dwindling Episcopalian population left its pews increasingly empty in the 1890s, St. George's, with Morgan's approval, became a leader in the Social Gospel movement. It survived by de-emphasizing doctrine and offering secular educational and recreational programs, enlisting thousands of young people from the nearby tenements.

beats.script_body: On Sunday, April 18, 1920, a neighborhood anarchist named Thomas W. Simpkin tried to assassinate J. P. Morgan Jr. outside St. George's. Incensed by the younger Morgan's anti-Communist remarks, Simpkin attempted to ambush him as he left Sunday Mass. In a case of mistaken identity, Simpkin instead tragically shot and killed Dr. James Markee, the Morgan family doctor. Five months later, the bombing of the Morgan Bank on Wall Street was widely assumed to be another anarchist attack aimed at Morgan.

Five months later, the bombing of the Morgan Bank on Wall Street was widely assumed to be another "anarchist attack" aimed at Morgan.

beats.script_body: On the northwest corner of Seventeenth Street and Second Avenue stands the former Manhattan General Hospital Building, the most impressive of the hospital buildings bordering Stuyvesant Square. Completed in 1902 with money donated by J. P. Morgan and designed by Robert H. Richardson, it originally housed the New York Lying-In Hospital — once the largest maternity hospital in the United States, serving the impoverished Lower East Side and often letting its bills go uncollected. Viewed in philanthropic circles as Morgan's personal charity, it struggled to find other benefactors and turned to Morgan each year to cover its deficit, becoming one of his most expensive ventures. Today the building houses luxury apartments and medical offices.

beats.script_body: The New York City Draft Riots of July 1863 were the largest and most destructive urban riots in American history, killing at least 105 people, and the greatest uprising of Americans against their government short of the Confederacy's secession. They sprang from the resentment of New York's working classes — especially Irish immigrants — toward the Civil War draft, made worse by a clause allowing the rich to buy a $300 substitute, condemned as 'a rich man's war, but a poor man's fight.' On Monday, July 13, protestors smashed the lottery wheel at the Third Avenue draft house, and by midmorning a full-scale riot had erupted. The rioters targeted symbols of the war, Republican leaders, and African Americans: at least eleven black men were lynched, and the Colored Orphan Asylum on Fifth Avenue was torched, its 237 children left to flee. A mob of thousands besieged the Union Steam Works, a former wire factory converted to arms production; twice they seized thousands of weapons before the Metropolitan Police and the Twelfth New York Infantry, firing howitzers down Second Avenue, fought them out. Rather than surrender, the rioters burned the five-story building to the ground, killing ten of their own trapped inside. The next day, five regiments diverted from Gettysburg arrived; the 152nd New York Volunteers camped in Stuyvesant Square while the Eighth Regiment Artillery encamped in Gramercy Park, and by Thursday order was restored.

In the end, rather than surrender the factory, the rioters burned the five-story brick building to the ground, killing ten of their own who remained trapped inside. The next day, July 15, five regiments of the Union Army, diverted directly from the battle of Gettysburg, began to arrive in the city. The 152 New York Volunteers established their camp in Stuyvesant Square, while the Eighth Regiment Artillery Troop encamped in Gramercy Park. By Thursday, July 16, order was restored.

beats.script_body: To a remarkable degree, the Gramercy Park neighborhood has stayed true to the vision of its founder, Samuel Ruggles, providing a striking contrast to the noisy commercial districts around it. When Ruggles took possession of Gramercy Seat in 1831, it was a mixture of swampland and small hills. The name 'Gramercy,' some believe, is a corruption of an old Dutch phrase, krom moerasje, meaning 'little crooked swamp;' others say it comes from crommessie vly, meaning 'knife-shaped swamp.' Whatever the case, Ruggles filled in the swamp in the 1830s with soil from the leveling of the nearby Bowery Hill. When he drew up the deed to the park in 1831, he provided for five trustees, regularly elected by the neighborhood, to maintain the grounds to his precise specifications; he laid out the pathways himself and had fifty different trees and shrubs planted. The eight-foot iron fence has stood around it since it officially opened in 1844. Gramercy Park was also one of the first New York developments to impose building restrictions: Ruggles's deed permitted only 'brick or stone dwellings' and barred any 'slaughter house, smith shop,' 'brewery, distillery, public museum,' or 'circus.' Today it is the only private park left in New York City.

beats.script_body: From the 1850s until the 1870s, Gramercy Park ranked among the city's most fashionable neighborhoods. It lost status after the Third Avenue Elevated Railroad was built close by in 1878. Though many residents left, those who stayed were influential enough to persuade Governor David Hill to veto a measure that would have run a cable-car line on Lexington Avenue through the park in 1890, and several later proposals to cut a road through the park were defeated. Since the 1940s most of the townhouses have been converted into apartments, and by the 1980s Gramercy Park had once again become a fashionable neighborhood, home to many celebrities.

beats.script_body: Both 15 and 16 Gramercy Park South, completed in 1845, were among the original townhouses on the square. No. 15 today houses the National Arts Club, but in the 1870s and 1880s it was the home of Samuel J. Tilden — 1874 New York governor and 1876 presidential candidate, whose career was built on bringing down the Tweed ring. Fearing disgruntled Tammany henchmen, Tilden built an underground tunnel from his house to Nineteenth Street as an escape route. When he died in 1886, he left a vast book collection and an estate exceeding $5 million to New York City specifically for a new public library — and when the New York Public Library's headquarters opened in 1911, his books were combined with the Astor and Lenox collections to form its original holdings.

beats.script_body: At 16 Gramercy Park South is the Players Club, founded by Edwin Booth in 1888. Widely considered the greatest actor of his generation, Booth came from a family of distinguished actors that included his unstable brother, John Wilkes Booth. Devastated by Lincoln's assassination at his brother's hand, Booth vowed never to appear in public again and resigned from his starring role in Hamlet; friends and admirers persuaded him to return nine months later, where New York society greeted him with an outpouring of sympathy. The acting profession was not highly regarded in nineteenth-century America, and perhaps because of his own family history, Booth felt the stigma deeply and endeavored to raise actors to 'a higher social grade than the Bohemian level.' He conceived the Players Club as a genteel society where actors could mix with the more cultivated, and in 1887 enlisted his friend Stanford White to remodel the facade with a portico and balcony. Founding members included Mark Twain and General William T. Sherman. At the center of Gramercy Park stands a statue of Edwin Booth as Hamlet, erected by the Players Club in 1918.

beats.script_body: At 19–20 Gramercy Park South is the former Sonnenberg mansion, a brick townhouse built in 1845 but altered many times since. When the Sonnenberg estate put it up for sale in 1979, the New Yorker's Brendan Gill called it 'unquestionably the greatest house remaining in private hands in New York.' Originally four stories, it gained a fifth floor and mansard roof in the 1850s, and in 1887 it was remodeled inside by McKim, Mead and White. In 1931, publicity man Benjamin Sonnenberg bought the house along with the apartment complex next door at No. 20, installed connecting doors, and turned No. 20's studio apartments into guest rooms — bringing his mansion to thirty-seven rooms. It remains a private home today.

beats.script_body: At 144 East Twentieth Street, off the southeast corner of the square, is the Brotherhood Synagogue, formerly the Friends Meeting House, built in 1859. Its Italianate architecture is almost identical to Henry Ward Beecher's 1849 Plymouth Church in Brooklyn Heights. Rescued from demolition by the Landmarks Commission in the 1960s, it was bought in 1975 by the Brotherhood Synagogue for $425,000. A Holocaust memorial stands on the east side of the building.

beats.script_body: The first cooperative apartment in New York City, 34 Gramercy Park East, was designed by architect George da Cunha. Opened in 1883, this gorgeous brick building with red terra-cotta ornamentation originally held twenty-seven apartments, three per floor, of seven to twelve rooms each. Abundant amenities were offered to attract a 'better' class of residents, including a gourmet restaurant owned by Louis Sherry on the eighth floor. The original gaslights flank the entrance, and the hydraulic elevators inside, the first in the city, still function. Next door at No. 36, another early cooperative designed by James Riley Gordon in 1910 carries whimsical medieval ornament in white terra-cotta, with monks, gargoyles, and cherubs, its front entrance guarded by two cast-stone knights in armor.

beats.script_body: Near the northern entrance to the park, a number of prominent New Yorkers made their homes. At 1 Lexington Avenue lived the daring entrepreneur Cyrus West Field, who conceived and organized the laying of the first undersea transatlantic cable, establishing telegraph communication between London and New York. After several disappointments, the cable finally became operable in 1865, making Field a national hero; he also built much of Manhattan's elevated railroads in the 1870s. Next door, at 9 Lexington Avenue, lived his friend and supporter Peter Cooper, one of New York's most beloved citizens and an inventor of extraordinary talents. Cooper created America's first steam locomotive, the 'Tom Thumb,' produced the first steel rails, and invented household products including glue and gelatin. Never having had a higher education himself, he founded Cooper Union, a free university for the working classes, which still runs tuition-free thanks chiefly to his endowment of nearly $1 million.

beats.script_body: Architect Stanford White lived along Gramercy Park North from 1901 to 1906. One of the greatest and most prolific architects of his time, White designed lavish mansions, churches, clubhouses, and monuments all over New York, and was a serious collector who imported antiques to furnish his home. Yet he is best remembered today not for his architecture but for the scandalous circumstances of his death, the site of which the tour visits later.

beats.script_body: At the corner of East Twenty-first Street and Park Avenue stands Calvary Church, once the prestigious parish of the Roosevelt, Vanderbilt, and Astor families, now assimilated into St. George's Parish of Stuyvesant Square. When this impressive brownstone church was completed in 1848, it heightened the appeal of the Gramercy Park area and prompted the sale of several of Samuel Ruggles's still-vacant lots. Its architect, James Renwick Jr., also designed Grace Church and St. Patrick's Cathedral. Both Edith Wharton and Eleanor Roosevelt were baptized at Calvary. The church is best viewed from across the street, where the empty base of one of its two original wooden steeples can be seen; the steeples were taken down after repeated lightning strikes.
